title: Separate scaling, failover, and restore paths
description: Choose an operating condition. Active routes show which endpoint, instance, shared storage, or independent recovery copy the application actually depends on.

nodes.label: Application
nodes.detail: Uses the cluster endpoint for writes and deliberately distributes read connections. It must recreate failed connections and keep retried operations idempotent.

nodes.label: Cluster endpoint
nodes.detail: Resolves to the current primary instance and follows a promoted writer after failover. Existing connections still need to be re-established.

nodes.label: Reader endpoint
nodes.detail: Routes new connections among available replicas. It does not balance individual queries over already-open long-lived connections.

nodes.label: Writer · AZ A
nodes.detail: Coordinates every write and can also serve reads. A cluster has one primary writer at a time.

nodes.label: Reader · AZ B
nodes.detail: Serves read-only queries and can be promoted. Match the writer's instance class and use a low promotion tier when rapid takeover matters.

nodes.label: Reader · AZ C
nodes.detail: Adds another read connection target and failure domain. It shares the cluster volume rather than maintaining an independent application-level backup.

nodes.label: Cluster volume
nodes.detail: Stores graph statements, indexes, dictionaries, and transaction metadata. Instance replicas attach to this same distributed volume.

nodes.label: Continuous backup
nodes.detail: Retains incremental restore data for the configured one-to-35-day window. A manual snapshot is needed for longer retention.

nodes.label: Restored cluster
nodes.detail: A restore creates a new cluster. Instances, custom parameter groups, security groups, validation, and application cutover must be handled explicitly.

nodes.label: Global secondary
nodes.detail: A Neptune global database secondary can be detached and promoted after a primary-Region outage. It must exist and be monitored before the incident.

scenarios.label: Healthy write
scenarios.summary: The application resolves the cluster endpoint to the single writer. The writer updates the shared cluster volume, whose storage segments are replicated across three Availability Zones.
scenarios.result: One instance coordinates writes; six-way storage replication protects the volume but does not create another writer or an independent logical backup.

scenarios.label: Scale reads
scenarios.summary: New reader-endpoint connections can resolve to either read replica. Long-lived connections do not rebalance each query, so the application must recycle or directly balance connections when distribution matters.
scenarios.result: Read replicas add query capacity and failover targets while all instances continue to use the same cluster storage volume.

scenarios.label: Writer failure
scenarios.summary: The AZ A writer is unavailable. Neptune promotes the cross-AZ reader, and the cluster endpoint begins resolving to that new writer.
scenarios.result: Requests can fail briefly during promotion. Clients must discard stale connections, resolve the cluster endpoint again, and retry only operations that are safe to repeat.

scenarios.label: Accidental delete
scenarios.summary: A valid delete is written to the shared volume and its storage copies. Availability replicas preserve the new, wrong state; recovery must use retained backup data.
scenarios.result: Restore to a new cluster at a point before the delete, recreate the required instances and controls, verify graph invariants, then cut the application over.

scenarios.label: Regional outage
scenarios.summary: The primary Region and all three local Availability Zones are unavailable. A local replica cannot help; only a pre-created cross-Region recovery design changes the path.
scenarios.result: For a Neptune global database, operators choose a secondary, detach and promote it, redirect writes, and prevent split brain. RTO and RPO must be measured in rehearsals.
